title: Release of Livery Stable Blues and playing with Broadway stars
summary: The records came out in May, and he describes entertaining troops and sharing bills with Caruso and Jolson.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And did Columbia issue those records? That's another question.

They didn't issue them till May, till the Liber Stable Blues became a national hit. It was all over the world, even down in Honolulu. And all the way the American forces went, they were carried overseas by the American troops, which we entertained over a million men. I had pastors to every fort and every hospital in New York. And we entertained the soldiers and sailors. I played on the bills with Caruso. I played on the bills with Jolson. I played on bills with Eddie Cantor. In fact, Eddie Cantor used to work downstairs in the Kidder Review for Gus Edwards. I played with Red Heart Mama, what's her name? Sophie Cousin. No. Yeah, I played two times with the same boss with her, but not with her. I played once at Rideswell. It was in 1919 when she was supposed to come in the fourth of 400 room. And they put her into Paradise and left her, stayed there until our time to go to England. See? Those people were good to us because we made business for them. We made fortune for them. They never got a cover charge before until the Dixon Land Jazz Band, where they got a dollar a cover. They paid nothing to us. We earned money for them. They didn't pay anything to us. They made money, made a fortune on us. You had to pay a cover and have a card to come in there. In other words, you was a member of the 400 Club. That was exclude the riff raff and the cheap customers out. Because the more popular music was getting, the more the riff raff was coming to get in on it. So they formed a club. You would have to have a card to get in. You would see that in the file, there were a card in there. And where was that? Well, Mae West. She was one? I played on Bill. Sure, I got him right in there. He in there. When you go to them things, you'll say, I played with Eva and Billy Galleang. She came here. She's not from New Orleans. They give a great big spill in the paper. I'm a poor little digger boy on the other side of the tracks. I was headlining on the same bills with her. They didn't even know me. They didn't know who I was. I came back here in 1925. Nobody even noticed me. I never looked for notoriety. I never looked for nothing. I never looked for credit for nothing. I never went anywhere. I came here as a sick man. I had a nervous breakdown. I came here for my health. I hadn't made a lot of money. I came here almost at $100,000. The other boys didn't have that much because they used to go spend as with women. Run around here and there and spend it. And I saved mine. Because coming from a poor family and knowing there was only one opportunity in my life to make it. I was to make this one opportunity. The old addicts say, opportunity only knocks once. And I made the best of it. And I have it. I'm skipping the game. I'd like to tell you when Regis died, or before Regis was sick, that we had trouble getting a piano player to play the rhythm. The first time Billy Hollander, who had heard us for two years in an orchestra in the next room from where we played in Rines. He sat in there about four days until we had Harry Shields to come up. Who was the brother? Larry Shields.
